state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you explain why you think the range wouldn't change if all the plants were cut in half or grew by the same amount? Think about how the range is calculated and how changing all values by the same proportion might affect it.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I think the range is just the difference between the biggest and smallest numbers, right? So if I cut everything in half, the biggest and smallest would still be the same distance apart. But I’m not sure how adding 3 cm would change it. Can you help me understand that part?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you think of any examples from previous interventions where changing all values by the same proportion did affect the range? How might those examples apply to this situation with the plant heights?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher fails to address the student's specific misconception about proportional changes (the student correctly understands addition but incorrectly thinks halving preserves range), provides vague prompts about 'previous interventions' the student hasn't mentioned, and the student shows no improvement in understanding by the end.
score.justification_pass2: While the teacher uses questions throughout, they fail to address the student's specific misconception about cutting in half versus adding a constant, and in Turn 3 they ask about 'previous interventions' that don't exist in this dialogue rather than using a concrete counterexample to expose the flawed reasoning about proportional changes.
